name: Tessera Corponation Packet Dissociation Rig
description:
The Packet Dissociation Rig is a compact offensive and defensive hacking platform designed around a single foundational principle: any data transmission can be made functionally unreadable if its constituent packets are distributed across enough simultaneous channels with enough temporal jitter between them. The PDR does not encrypt in the conventional sense — it dissociates. Outgoing transmissions are shredded into micro-packets and distributed across dozens of simultaneous frequencies, protocols, and mesh relay nodes with randomized timing offsets. The receiving end, running complementary TESSERA firmware, reassembles them. To any intercepting system, the transmission looks like background noise across multiple unrelated channels.

The rig itself is a matte-black unit roughly the size of a hardback novel, with a fold-out antenna array and a physical interface port for direct-connect operations. Its processing core runs TESSERA's proprietary SCATTER architecture — a dynamic algorithm that continuously adjusts dissociation parameters based on the local signal environment, making the pattern of the transmission itself unpredictable even if an adversary has characterized the method. The rig can operate in passive mode, protecting the user's own transmissions, or in active mode, where it projects dissociation interference across a local area, degrading the coherence of nearby communications it does not control.

The PDR is the standard hacking rig for TESSERA's own field operatives and is sold at significant markup to corporate security firms and licensed government intelligence units. It has a well-developed black market presence because cracked firmware removes the mandatory TESSERA backdoor — a feature the company officially denies exists but which competing intelligence services have documented extensively. The cracked version is called a Ghost Rig and commands a substantial premium over the legitimate hardware.

specifications.supported_protocols: Mesh, cellular, short-range RF, encrypted corporate bands, legacy infrastructure
specifications.interface: Direct-connect physical port plus wireless pairing
specifications.battery_life: 6 hours active mode, 18 hours passive mode
specifications.firmware_update_requirement: Mandatory monthly via TESSERA network (legitimate units only)

tactical_use: Operatives use the PDR in passive mode during infiltration to ensure their comms and data pulls are invisible to corporate network monitoring. In active mode, it is deployed to degrade an adversary's coordination during an operation — disrupting their mesh communications without producing the obvious jamming signature that triggers hardened countermeasures. Direct-connect operations allow a skilled operator to interface with hardwired systems, dissociate security handshakes across multiple authentication channels simultaneously, and exploit the resulting desynchronization to force authentication failures. Black-market Ghost Rigs are preferred for operations where TESSERA's backdoor would compromise the mission.
cultural_context: Owning a legitimate PDR is a marker of serious corporate or government standing — the licensing process is invasive and the cost is prohibitive for most. The Ghost Rig version occupies a different cultural space entirely: it is a status symbol among high-end freelance operatives, a proof of technical sophistication and access to networks that can source and flash the cracked firmware. TESSERA publicly pursues Ghost Rig users aggressively, but the consensus in operational circles is that the company also uses Ghost Rig tracking as an intelligence tool — allowing cracked units to operate long enough to map the networks using them.
story_hooks: A Ghost Rig surfaces with firmware that appears to be a genuine cracked version but contains a second-layer backdoor more sophisticated than TESSERA's standard — someone is running a honeypot operation targeting the people who buy Ghost Rigs to avoid TESSERA surveillance.

The players' PDR begins receiving reassembled transmissions it should not have access to, suggesting someone else in their operational area is running a complementary TESSERA unit and inadvertently routing packets through their rig.

A licensed PDR recovered from a corporate operative has its mandatory firmware update log intact — and the update timestamps reveal that TESSERA was pushing real-time location data from the unit during a period when the operative was supposedly running a black-site operation their employer denies authorizing.

A TESSERA engineer approaches the players claiming to have documented the backdoor and wanting to go public — they need the players to extract the evidence from a TESSERA facility while using PDRs that TESSERA can monitor.
